questions.question: Which statement best describes an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in a VPC?
options: A logical component in a VPC that represents a virtual network card
A subnet-level routing table that controls traffic between subnets
A Region-wide gateway that connects a VPC to the internet
A block storage volume that can be attached to one EC2 instance
questions.explanation: An ENI is defined as a logical component in a VPC that represents a virtual network card. A route table is a separate VPC construct for directing traffic, not an interface. An internet gateway is a VPC component for internet connectivity, not a network card. An EBS volume is block storage and has no network identity.

questions.question: A company attaches an ENI to an instance and wants maximum flexibility for IP addressing on that interface. Which combination of private IPv4 addresses can the ENI have?
options: One primary private IPv4 and one or more secondary private IPv4 addresses
One primary private IPv4 only, because secondaries require a new ENI
Multiple primary private IPv4 addresses and no secondary addresses
One primary private IPv4 and exactly one optional secondary private IPv4
questions.explanation: An ENI has exactly one primary private IPv4 and can carry one or more secondary private IPv4 addresses. Restricting it to a primary only is wrong because secondaries are supported. Multiple primaries is wrong because there is one primary per ENI. Limiting secondaries to exactly one contradicts the one-or-more rule.

questions.question: An architect wants several public-facing addresses on a single ENI, each pair made of a private IPv4 and an Elastic IP. What is the correct rule?
options: Each private IPv4 on the ENI can be associated with one Elastic IP
A single private IPv4 can carry multiple Elastic IPs for scale
Elastic IPs attach to the subnet, not to addresses on the ENI
Elastic IPs and public IPv4 addresses are the same ENI attribute
questions.explanation: The ENI attribute is one Elastic IP (IPv4) per private IPv4, so additional addresses require additional private IPv4s. Attaching several Elastic IPs to one private IPv4 violates the pairing rule. Elastic IPs associate per private IPv4 on the interface, not at subnet level. The ENI's single public IPv4 is listed separately from Elastic IP associations.

questions.question: A solutions architect reviews the IP attributes listed for an ENI and needs to state how many public IPv4 addresses it can have. Which answer is correct?
options: One public IPv4 address
One public IPv4 address per secondary private IPv4
No public IPv4 address, because only Elastic IPs are allowed
A maximum of four public IPv4 addresses, one per security group
questions.explanation: The ENI attribute list includes one public IPv4 address. Scaling public IPv4s with the number of secondaries is an invented rule. Elastic IPs are an additional attribute, not a replacement for a public IPv4. Security groups are traffic filters and have no relation to public address count.

questions.question: An instance's network interface is detached and attached to a replacement instance. Which configuration element follows the ENI automatically?
options: Its MAC address and its one or more security groups
The instance profile and IAM role of the original instance
The EBS volumes containing the operating system
The subnet route table entries of the original instance
questions.explanation: An ENI has a MAC address and one or more attached security groups that travel with it when moved. IAM instance profiles belong to the instance, not the interface. EBS volumes are separate storage attachments. Route tables are subnet-level and are unaffected by moving an interface.

questions.question: An application server fails. The team needs the standby instance to take over the same private IP, Elastic IP, MAC address and security groups with no client reconfiguration. What should they do?
options: Detach the secondary ENI from the failed instance and attach it to the standby instance in the same AZ
Launch a new instance in the same subnet and reassign the security groups manually
Change the route table to point the Elastic IP at the standby instance
Terminate the failed instance so its addresses are released, then recreate them
questions.explanation: Moving the ENI carries its private IPs, Elastic IP associations, MAC address and security groups, which is the ENI failover pattern. A new instance with manually reassigned security groups loses the existing network identity. Route tables do not reassociate Elastic IPs. Terminating and recreating addresses changes the identity and is slower.
questions.keyTopic: Move ENI between instances for failover

questions.question: A team plans cross-AZ failover by detaching an ENI from a failed instance in AZ A and attaching it to a standby instance in AZ B. Why will this plan not work?
options: An ENI is bound to a specific Availability Zone and can only attach to instances in that AZ
An ENI can be moved only after the source instance is terminated
An ENI's MAC address must be reassigned whenever it crosses subnets
An ENI can be attached to only one instance in its entire lifetime
questions.explanation: The ENI is bound to one Availability Zone, so failover by moving it is limited to instances in that same AZ. Termination of the source is not required for moving. The MAC address travels with the ENI rather than being reassigned. An ENI can be detached and re-attached repeatedly, not once.
questions.keyTopic: ENI bound to a single AZ

questions.question: How does the primary ENI (Eth0) compare with a secondary ENI (Eth1) when planning failover?
options: Eth0 is the instance's original interface carrying the primary private IP, while Eth1 is separately created and can be moved for failover
Eth0 can be detached and moved to another instance, while Eth1 is permanently fixed
Both interfaces are created automatically with the instance and cannot be moved
Eth1 carries the primary private IP, while Eth0 carries only secondary addresses
questions.explanation: Eth0 is the interface the instance was created with and carries its primary private IP, whereas the separately created secondary ENI is the unit typically moved for failover. Reversing which interface is movable is incorrect. Secondary ENIs are created independently, not automatically with the instance. The primary private IP belongs to Eth0, not Eth1.
questions.keyTopic: Move ENI between instances for failover

questions.question: A design requires an interface that exists before any instance does and can be attached to a running instance later without terminating it. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Create the ENI independently of any instance and attach it on the fly
Create the instance first and add a second private IP to its Eth0
Place the instance in a public subnet and assign it an Elastic IP
Attach a second EBS volume and configure it as a network device
questions.explanation: An ENI can be created independently and attached or moved onto running instances. Adding a secondary private IP does not create a separately movable interface. Elastic IPs are addresses, not interfaces. EBS volumes are block storage and cannot act as network interfaces.
questions.keyTopic: Move ENI between instances for failover
